In Taiwan it is used in gezaixi (Taiwanese opera), in gezai storytelling, in folk storytelling and in Beiguan music, and it accompanies sung Hengchun folk tunes such as 《四季春》 (Four Seasons Spring). In southern Fujian it accompanies gezai and gezaixi opera; Japanese seigaku favours the short-necked yueqin, while mingaku uses the long-necked one. Modern works include Liu Xijin's 《北方民族生活素描》 (Sketches of Northern Peoples' Life) and 《鐵人之歌》 (Song of the Iron Man), Sui Lijun's 《北大荒狂想曲》 (Rhapsody of the Great Northern Wilderness) and Meng Qingbiao's 《樹上的搖籃》 (Cradle in the Tree) and 《阿瑪架》 (Amajia); the sources also list a video of Fang Jinlong playing 《情深誼長》 (Deep Feeling, Long Friendship).

The yueqin is a traditional plucked instrument that comes from China and has spread through East Asia. It belongs to the lute family, classification number 321.322. It usually has a round resonating body, a short neck and high frets, with four strings as a rule, though some have two or three; the traditional silk strings have mostly given way to nylon. You stop the strings with the left hand and pluck with a plectrum in the right, and in Peking opera a small wooden stick is used instead. The yueqin comes from the ruan and later became an independent instrument; it is widely used in the Peking opera orchestra, where it often takes the melodic part, and it also appears in Taiwanese gezaixi, gezai storytelling, folk storytelling and Japanese seigaku and similar settings.
月琴源出中國阮，早期與阮琴同名混用，唐代起有現名，北宋文獻已記其形制。晉代流行，: The yueqin comes from the Chinese ruan and was long confused with it under the same name; the present name appears from the Tang dynasty, and Northern Song documents already record its shape. It was popular in the Jin dynasty and later reached Japan and Vietnam; in Japan it flourished in the 1830s, was banned during the Second World War and came back afterwards. In the Qing dynasty the short-necked form appeared, better suited to high notes and to opera accompaniment. In the mid-twentieth century mainland China established the short-necked yueqin as an independent instrument, separate from the ruan; Taiwan, influenced by Ming and Qing and by Japanese yueqin, developed a more varied set of types and playing traditions.
月琴演奏時左手按弦、右手持撥子彈奏；傳統撥子長而尖，現代也常用吉他撥片。京劇月琴: You stop the strings with the left hand and pluck with a plectrum in the right; the traditional plectrum is long and pointed, and a guitar pick is also common today. The Peking opera yueqin uses a small wooden stick instead and plays only in first position, so the melody has to move in octaves. The northern yueqin has bamboo for both front and back, and the player must hold the body away from the chest; the southern yueqin has a longer neck and freer intonation. Beginners first tune in perfect fifths or in unison, then practise stopping the strings at the high frets: because the frets stand high, the fingers never touch the body, which helps timbre and intonation, though chords are harder.
月琴為中國傳統撥弦樂器，流傳於東亞，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 32: The yueqin is a traditional Chinese plucked instrument found across East Asia, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322. The body is usually a round wooden soundbox, sometimes octagonal; on Taiwanese yueqin the soundboard is often paulownia, and the northern yueqin uses bamboo for the front and back plates. The sound source is the strings, traditionally silk, now mostly nylon, with fishing line also popular in Taiwan. Inside the soundbox you can see a metal wire or a metal coil, and the Peking opera yueqin uses a small wooden stick while modern players use a pick. The materials of the soundbars, the soundpost and the other parts are not recorded.
月琴音色被描述為清脆柔和、分明而銜接流暢，其發聲來自圓形空心面板與音箱內一端固定: The yueqin's timbre is described as crisp and soft, distinct yet smoothly joined. It sounds from the round hollow soundboard and from the metal wire fixed at one end inside the soundbox, which resonates in a particular way. The short-necked yueqin has a range of about two octaves and is mostly tuned high; volume varies with the type, and Chinese sources call it small, though a comparison within the family says the yueqin can be very loud, one instrument drowning out a whole Chinese orchestra. It is plucked with a plectrum, a small wooden stick or a guitar pick; the northern yueqin must be held away from the body, and some southern ones use a metal coil inside the soundbox to raise the volume. Compared with the ruan, the yueqin has no bridge and only one small soundhole, its timbre falls between the ruan and the pipa, and it is used mainly in the high register.
